item.title: The Last Signal: Back at the Friday Table
item.description: The question at the heart of this series came up on one of those late Friday afternoons when the week finally lets go. A few of us around a table, coffee going cold, asking a question most of us carried but rarely said out loud: why do so many people doing genuine enterprise-level thinking never actually hold the EA...

item.title: The Team Stopped Raising Risks. The Survey Said Culture.
item.description: A programme goes amber in week nine. It reaches the steering committee in week fourteen, red, with a question attached: why wasn’t this flagged earlier?

item.title: The Team Inherited an AI Capability. The Org Chart Stayed the Same.
item.description: A platform team already carrying a full delivery load gets a line added to its charter: AI-enabled. The slide calls it an uplift. The team calls it Tuesday.

item.title: The Demo Proved It Could. The Decision System Never Got Asked.
item.description: There’s a slide near the front of most strategy decks now. “AI-First Organisation.” Bullet points about agentic workflows, augmented decision-making, intelligent automation across the value chain. The board nods. Everyone in the room agrees this is the direction.

item.title: The Demo Proved It Could. Nobody Asked If It Should.
item.description: The pitch runs forty minutes. The model handles the sample data cleanly, answers the planted questions, and someone says the word “transformative” before the deck finishes. Three weeks later there’s a pilot, a budget line, and a delivery date. Nobody has written down what the pilot is meant to prove.

item.title: Why I Write It Down
item.description: Twelve posts. None of them about me. That was deliberate — the failures I was describing weren’t mine to claim, and the mechanism mattered more than the messenger.

item.title: What This Series Has Actually Been About
item.description: Twelve posts. Different rooms, different vendors, different failures. If you’ve read them as a string of separate stories, here’s the thing they were all doing underneath: showing you the same mechanism, wearing a different uniform each time.

item.title: The Cost of Being Early / The Cost of Being Late
item.description: She flagged the concentration risk in the vendor portfolio eleven months before the vendor had an outage. No incident. No number. Just a pattern she’d seen twice before, at two other employers, in the sourcing data.

item.title: The Person Who Was Right, Eventually
item.description: The migration review is the fourth one this quarter. Same room, same slide, same architect raising the same objection.

item.title: The Person Who Knew
item.description: The capability workshop runs the way it always runs. Twelve people around a table, a facilitator with a shared screen, a map with forty boxes waiting for a colour.

item.title: The Convenient Unknown
item.description: The number has sat in the steering pack for two years: eighty per cent mapped, risk rated low. Nobody built it. Everybody uses it. Then the cutover weekend arrives, six on Saturday morning. The delivery lead is on. The vendor is on. Someone from the original business case is on, camera off, mic on mute.

item.title: Who Called the EA?
item.description: The incident starts at eleven on a Tuesday night. By midnight there is a bridge call. The platform lead is on. The vendor is on. An engineer who left the programme eight months ago is on, because somebody still had her number and knew the integration layer lived in her head.

item.title: The Gap Between the Map and the Ground
item.description: The map says the landscape is understood. The ground says otherwise.

item.title: The Decaying Map
item.description: That Friday conversation was honest. Here’s the part we didn’t say out loud.

item.title: The Map and the Territory
item.description: It was one of those late Friday afternoons when the week finally lets go. A few of us — architects and engineers with years of real delivery — sitting around a table, coffee going cold, talking honestly.

item.title: Organisational Amnesia: The Second Kind
item.description: Some organisations don’t move too fast. They move too carefully, and arrive at the same failure by a different route.

item.title: Organisational Amnesia: The First Kind
item.description: There are two kinds of organisations failing at AI governance right now. They look nothing alike. They have the same disease.

item.title: Executing a Guess
item.description: Cloud isn’t the hard part anymore. Execution is.
